stem: Your support agent calls the Messages API with tools defined. The response has stop_reason "tool_use" and a tool_use block requesting lookup_order. What must the client do next to continue the agent loop correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: Send a new user message containing a tool_result block whose tool_use_id matches the tool_use block, then call the API again

options.label: B
options.text: Re-send the same request unchanged until stop_reason becomes "end_turn"

options.label: C
options.text: Append an assistant message with the tool output and call the API again

options.label: D
options.text: Set tool_choice to "none" and resend so Claude stops asking for tools

explanation: Tool results are returned to Claude as a user-role message containing a tool_result content block whose tool_use_id matches the requested tool_use. The loop continues until stop_reason is "end_turn". Tool output is never an assistant message, and resending unchanged just repeats the request.

stem: The agent sometimes answers from memory instead of calling the account-status tool, occasionally giving stale info. You want it to always consult a tool before responding on account questions. Which change most directly enforces that?

options.label: A
options.text: Set tool_choice to "any" so the model must call some tool before producing a final answer

options.label: B
options.text: Lower temperature to 0

options.label: C
options.text: Remove the tool definitions so Claude cannot guess

options.label: D
options.text: Set tool_choice to {"type":"none"}

explanation: tool_choice "any" forces Claude to invoke a tool rather than reply directly, ensuring a lookup happens. "none" forbids tools (opposite effect); removing tools breaks the lookup entirely; temperature does not control tool invocation.

stem: A team wants a reusable /refactor command available to everyone who clones the repo, accepting the target file as an argument. What is the correct setup?

options.label: A
options.text: Create .claude/commands/refactor.md in the repo, write the prompt body, and reference $ARGUMENTS for the file path

options.label: B
options.text: Add a refactor key to package.json scripts

options.label: C
options.text: Put the prompt in ~/.claude/commands/refactor.md so it is personal-only

options.label: D
options.text: Define it as an MCP tool named refactor

explanation: Project slash commands are markdown files in the committed .claude/commands/ directory; the filename becomes the command name and $ARGUMENTS injects user input. ~/.claude/commands is personal (not shared via the repo). npm scripts and MCP tools are different mechanisms.

stem: A lead agent dispatches several research subagents in parallel. The orchestrator's context keeps overflowing as subagents return long transcripts. What is the best architectural fix?

options.label: A
options.text: Have each subagent return only a concise synthesized summary with citations, not its full working transcript

options.label: B
options.text: Increase max_tokens on the orchestrator request

options.label: C
options.text: Run all research in the single orchestrator agent instead

options.label: D
options.text: Disable tool use in subagents

explanation: The orchestrator-worker pattern's benefit is context isolation: subagents do the heavy lifting in their own windows and return condensed results. Returning full transcripts defeats that. Collapsing back to one agent or raising max_tokens does not solve context bloat.

stem: You need Claude to return a changelog as JSON with fixed fields for an automated release pipeline. Which approach gives the most reliable schema-conformant output?

options.label: A
options.text: Define a tool whose input_schema is the changelog JSON Schema and force it via tool_choice {"type":"tool","name":...}

options.label: B
options.text: Ask in the prompt for JSON and hope formatting is consistent

options.label: C
options.text: Raise temperature so outputs vary less

options.label: D
options.text: Use the Message Batches API

explanation: Forcing a tool call with a JSON Schema makes the model emit schema-validated structured input, the most reliable structured-output technique. Free-text JSON requests are brittle; temperature does not enforce structure; Batches affects cost/latency, not schema conformance.

stem: You want Claude Code to triage failing tests inside a CI job and emit machine-readable results without any interactive prompts, while preventing destructive shell actions. Which configuration is appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Run claude -p with --output-format json and restrict capability with allowed-tools / permission settings

options.label: B
options.text: Run claude in interactive mode and pipe "yes" to confirm prompts

options.label: C
options.text: Grant full permissions and parse the human-readable terminal output with regex

options.label: D
options.text: Use the Messages API directly because Claude Code cannot run in CI

explanation: Headless mode (claude -p) with a JSON output format is the supported non-interactive path; tool allow-listing/permission modes constrain side effects so automation is safe. Interactive mode and unrestricted permissions are unsafe and fragile in CI; Claude Code does support headless CI use.

stem: You must extract structured fields from 200,000 archived PDFs. Latency is not important but cost is. Which API choice best fits?

options.label: A
options.text: The Message Batches API, which processes large batches asynchronously at about 50% lower cost with results typically within 24 hours

options.label: B
options.text: Standard synchronous Messages API calls in a tight loop for fastest turnaround

options.label: C
options.text: Streaming responses to reduce token cost

options.label: D
options.text: The Files API, because it makes extraction free

explanation: The Message Batches API is purpose-built for high-volume, latency-tolerant work: roughly 50% cheaper than standard requests with results generally available within 24 hours. Streaming does not lower token cost; the Files API stores inputs but does not change pricing.

stem: Across thousands of extractions, a small fraction of responses are not valid against your JSON Schema. What is the most robust production handling?

options.label: A
options.text: Validate every result against the schema and, on failure, retry the request (optionally with a corrective message) before surfacing an error

options.label: B
options.text: Assume forced tool calls are always schema-valid and skip validation

options.label: C
options.text: Lower max_tokens so responses are shorter and cannot be malformed

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to free-text output and parse heuristically

explanation: Even with forced tool calls, you should validate outputs and implement retry/repair for the small failure tail; reliability comes from validation plus retry, not from assuming perfection. Shorter responses and heuristic free-text parsing increase, not decrease, failure risk.
